procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated October 16, 1968 of the Madras High Court in Criminal Misc. Petition No. 980 of 1968.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellants filed applications in the High Court under s. 561A, Criminal Procedure Code, for quashing the proceedings in the Magistrate's court, but the applications were dismissed.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants appealed to the Supreme Court from the High Court's order dismissing their applications to quash the proceedings. The Supreme Court allowed the appeals, set aside the High Court's order, and quashed the prosecution proceedings against the appellants.

directions: The order of the High Court rejecting the applications under s. 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure is set aside.
The proceedings for the prosecution of the appellants are quashed.

issue.issue_text: Whether the complaint filed by the Director of Enforcement was invalid for failing to comply with the mandatory condition in the proviso to Section 23D(1) of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1947, which requires the Director to form an opinion, based on material from an enquiry, that the imposable penalty would be inadequate before filing a criminal complaint.

facts: The Director of Enforcement initiated an enquiry under Section 23D(1) of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1947, by issuing a show-cause notice on August 25, 1967.
Subsequently, the Director conducted investigations and took statements.
On March 17, 1968, the Director filed a criminal complaint against the accused instead of proceeding with the adjudication for a penalty.
The accused argued that the complaint was invalid because the Director had not complied with the pre-conditions set out in the proviso to Section 23D(1).
law: The Court interpreted Sections 23(1) and 23D(1) of the Act as needing to be read together.
It held that when a contravention occurs, the Director of Enforcement must first initiate adjudication proceedings for a penalty under the main clause of Section 23D(1).
The Director cannot, at his discretion, choose to file a criminal complaint from the outset.

The proviso to Section 23D(1) provides the only mechanism for filing a criminal complaint. This can only be done if, during the course of the formal enquiry, the Director forms an opinion, based on the circumstances of the case, that the penalty he is empowered to impose would be inadequate.
The Court described this requirement as a mandatory "safeguard" provided by the legislature to ensure that a person is not subjected to a more severe punishment at the "sweet-will" of the Director.
application: The Court examined the record to determine if the Director had complied with the mandatory conditions of the proviso to Section 23D(1).

It found no material on record to show that, during the formal enquiry initiated by the show-cause notice, the Director had come across any information that could lead him to form the opinion that the imposable penalty would be inadequate.
The Court distinguished between a general "investigation" and the formal "enquiry" required by the Act and the Adjudication Proceedings and Appeal Rules, 1957.

It concluded that any statements taken or investigations conducted were part of the investigation phase, not the formal enquiry. Since the accused had not yet shown cause and there was no consideration of it, the enquiry had not progressed to a stage where the necessary opinion could be formed based on materials from that enquiry.
Therefore, the Director failed to satisfy the condition precedent for filing a complaint.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the argument, holding that the complaint was invalid because it was filed without satisfying the mandatory requirement of the proviso to Section 23D(1). The Director of Enforcement had not formed the necessary opinion based on material gathered during a formal enquiry that the potential penalty would be inadequate. Consequently, the proceedings based on the invalid complaint were quashed.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the complaint filed by the Director of Enforcement was invalid for failing to comply with the mandatory condition in the proviso to Section 23D(1) of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1947, which requires the Director to form an opinion, based on material from an enquiry, that the imposable penalty would be inadequate before filing a criminal complaint.
appellant_arguments: The complaint was filed without satisfying the requirements of the proviso to Section 23D(1) of the Act.
There was no material before the Director of Enforcement, gathered during a formal enquiry, on which he could have formed the opinion that the penalty he was empowered to impose would be inadequate.
The statements recorded and investigations conducted were not part of a formal 'enquiry' as required by the Act and the Adjudication Proceedings and Appeal Rules, 1957.
The proper procedure for an enquiry, which includes considering the cause shown by the accused in response to a notice, was not followed.
respondent_arguments: A pleading filed by the appellant amounted to an admission that statements were taken and investigations were made during the enquiry.
This admission demonstrated that there was material on record from the enquiry, which the Director could have used to form the opinion that it was a fit case for making a complaint.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Where a statute provides for two alternative punishments for the same act, one of which is more severe, and the choice is left to an authority, such a provision would be void under Article 14 for conferring unguided discretion. To save the provision's validity, it must be interpreted to mean that the authority must first initiate the less severe proceeding (adjudication for a penalty) and can only resort to the more severe proceeding (filing a criminal complaint) if, during the initial proceeding, it determines that the penalty it is empowered to impose would be inadequate.
obiter: If a particular interpretation will ensure the validity of a law, that interpretation must be preferred.

A legal provision that provides for two alternative punishments for the same act, one differing from the other, without any limitations on the choice between them, would be void under Article 14 of the Constitution.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The complaint must be held to have been filed without satisfying the requirements and conditions of the proviso to s. 23D(l) of the Act, and must be held invalid. The court found that although an enquiry was initiated by a show-cause notice, the record does not show that any material came before the respondent during that enquiry which could be relevant for forming an opinion that the penalty he was empowered to impose would be inadequate. The statements that were recorded were in the course of an investigation, not in the course of an enquiry under s. 23D(l), and the proper procedure for an enquiry, such as considering the cause shown by the accused, was not followed.
legal_tests_applied: The Director of Enforcement must first initiate proceedings under the principal clause of s. 23D(1) for adjudication of penalty and is empowered to file a complaint in court only when, at any stage of the adjudication enquiry, he forms the opinion that the penalty he is empowered to impose would not be adequate.

The formation of the opinion under the proviso to Section 23D(1) must be based on material gathered during a formal 'enquiry' held in accordance with the Act and the Adjudication Proceedings and Appeal Rules, 1957, which is distinct from material gathered during an 'investigation'.
When a safeguard is provided by the Legislature before a person can be subjected to a severer punishment, the authority must strictly comply with all the conditions laid down by law.
policy_considerations: An interpretation of a law that will ensure its validity must be preferred; therefore, s. 23D(1) is interpreted to provide a guiding criterion for the Director's choice between adjudication and prosecution, thus saving it from being void for granting arbitrary discretion under Article 14 of the Constitution.

When a person is placed in greater jeopardy of being liable to a more severe punishment, it can only be done by strictly adhering to the procedural safeguards laid down by the legislature, such as the requirement to form a specific opinion based on an enquiry before initiating prosecution.
